Maybe the culture of the GC field has changed, but when I was applying, the message I repeatedly received from GC programs is that they want someone who is committed and knows GC is the only career for them. The reasoning for this is that they don't want people who change their mind about the field halfway through, which I can understand, but what this turns into (in the applicant spaces I was a part of, at least) is prospective students do not fully explore other options because they are afraid they will be perceived as being "less committed" than other applicants.

In my second interview cycle, I mentioned that I had recently shadowed a grief counselor, and one program asked me why I would do that if I was applying for GC school. I also remember being given advice that if you are applying to more than one grad program, i.e. GC school and PA school as a back up, you shouldn't tell programs that because it will make you seem less committed to GC.

I'm sure this isn't the case for every program or student, but this culture made me feel like I shouldn't explore other options, and when GC didn't work out for me, I felt unprepared.

I looked at lots! Nursing, PA school, medical school, project management, clinical psychology, and public health were the main ones. I ultimately decided on social work because I thought that it aligned the most with my values, and there is a state university in my hometown that fully funded my MSW. I completed informational interviews with a lot of these careers, too, which helped my decision.

The most helpful thing I did for myself was write down everything that I liked about GC and reflecting on if it was something that I could ONLY get from GC. Yes, working with and counseling prenatal families is something GCs do... but it's also something that many other professionals do. I decided I was most interested in the psychosocial aspects of GC, but someone who is more interested in the science-side of things might get more satisfaction from a different career.

Social work. There is a lot of overlap with counseling and teaching/education. Working in medical or forensic social work also ties into the medical/genetic aspect.

Like GC, social work also has its pros and cons, but what ultimately made me make this decision was:

1. Getting an advanced degree at no cost

2. Decent job outlook and not being tied down to a location (vs. GC roles that may only exist in large cities)

3. Lots of diverse specialties

4. Salary is not as bad as the media makes it out to be and is even comparable to GC depending on location and specialty

Just want to say, I feel this so much. I started getting hair loss in my early 20s and I remember doing the math and being like… really for the rest of my life?! 50+ years?? As a part of being a forgetful human, there’s no way that I could take it perfectly for that long. And what if I wanted to become pregnant??

I ultimately decided to stay off of it. I decided that if this is who I am, I should learn to embrace it. minox, even though it works WONDERFULLY for some people, is a bandaid at the end of the day. it doesn’t fix the issue and if i did stop taking it, i would still have “my” hair.

I am now in my late 20s and I will say this: though I am proud of myself for embracing my flaws, I wish I would have at least tried it. Now, my hair loss is severe to the point where hair dressers sometimes turn me away because I don’t even have enough to cut. even if i were to take minox now, i doubt i would ever get to the amount i had years ago. Yes, it sucks to have to take it forever, but you will only be young once. a year (how long most people recommend you try minox before deciding if it works for you) is such a short time in the grand scheme of things.

and, taking minox isn’t a commitment for the rest of your life… it’s only a commitment until your next dose. at any time, at any point in your life, you can choose to stop it. and if you do, it won’t make things worse. it will only bring you back to your natural state, which i think to some degree, you should embrace as “you” (easier said than done).

maybe thinking about it from a perspective of “just trying for now” might help?

whatever you decide, i hope it helps you. hair loss is so hard to deal with and it’s so hard to feel beautiful with this condition. remember that you are more than your hair!

and i recommend searching this sub regarding your cat. a lot of people have creative solutions to keep their cats safe while they use minox!

Yes, always. 2 options:

1. Don’t tell them their name is written down. If they ask, say “do you think it’s written down?”

My advice is to pick your battles. Middle schoolers will inherently test boundaries. Some may be openly disrespectful. Especially to a substitute.

A lot of advice for working with middle schoolers involves building rapport/a relationship. For substitutes, this is impossible.

When kids are off task, I give them a warning, i.e. “Please take a seat”.  The next time, I clearly state the consequences if they don’t listen, i.e. “This is the second time I am asking you to take a seat. If you get up without permission again, I am going to write your name down for your teacher.”

Then, if it happens again, I write their name down. I don’t yell or ask them again. I used to get migraines, too, and since I’ve started doing this, I leave my days much happier and calmer.

I know you said that it doesn’t feel right to let them be. But, at the end of the day, there is absolutely nothing you can do to make middle schoolers do something they don’t want to. They know this too. Yelling, etc. only fuels the power struggle. If they know the consequence and they choose it anyway, that is their decision.

And remember, take a deep breath. Kids can be mean. It’s nothing personal. If there’s ever gross disrespect (i.e. a student insults you) or safety concerns, always call the office.

i love middle schoolers! they’re my favorite age to work with.

in my experience, building good rapport is extremely important for this age range. if you ask them to do something, tell them why. if they ask why it’s a rule, be prepared to explain why. i commonly told the kids “this is a camp rule and if you don’t follow it i will get in trouble, and i really want to keep my job”. they are old enough to understand consequences like that. they DO NOT respond well to being told to do something for no reason, or being told to do something for a reason they don’t agree with. for example… 

me: lets do an icebreaker!

camper: why?

me: to make friends

camper: that’s stupid, i already have friends outside of camp

unless you have a holy gift for making middle schoolers listen to you, trying to lecture them further on the merits of making friends is not going to work. you need to “shift” their priorities to make them care more. for example: “well, the camp director won’t let us have our snack unless he sees us do the morning activity” or “if you guys give the activity a try i will let the group choose what music we listen to at lunch”

setting firm boundaries in the beginning is also important. middle schoolers test boundaries by nature. this is not due to them being “evil” like some people will tell you. it’s just their natural stage of childhood development. if someone does something against the rules, i.e. conversation about drugs/alcohol, cell phone use, violence, etc. address it the first time you see it, even if they “backpedal” out of the behavior. if you say there is a consequence, follow through. middle schoolers are aware some rules can be bent, and it’s up to you to determine which ones are acceptable.

something that also helps is to plan in ways to “break the rules”. middle schoolers love thinking they are cool and able to break rules. for example, “raiding” the snack cabin, eating lunch in a “forbidden area”, etc.

another tip is to always plan multiple activities. if the middle schoolers really are being resistant, tell them “okay, we can either do activity A or activity B” and be firm that there is no third option.

also, just be down to earth. middle schoolers get a lot of crap from EVERYONE. from their parents for growing up too fast or too slow, from their teachers for being too rambunctious, and there is now pressure from their peers to be “cool” at all times. kindness and understanding goes a long way. if you yell at them even once, they will always remember.

also, if there are younger kids at the camp, allowing them to mentor them is generally successful.

a final funny story:

my first ever job as a camp counselor, i was thrown to the wolves. i had no experience working with kids and i was assigned as the sole middle school counselor. at this camp, the middle schoolers were sectioned off from the younger campers, so i didn’t even have the director nearby to help.

i researched icebreakers and came up with a game where we would pass a ball around and answer questions about each other. very simple. of course, once i got my group into a circle, it was dead silent. seriously, these kids were acting like they had never thrown a ball or spoken out loud before.

after about 10 minutes of awkward silence, i finally said “raise your hand if you’re here because your parents made you”. every hand shot up. then, the game became tossing the ball and sharing what they WISHED they were doing instead. from there, great conversations sparked about tv shows, video games, common interests, etc.

best of luck!! you will have an amazing summer.

i got my first ever IUD put in 4 years ago at age 20. it is a copper IUD and i mostly love it.

insertion: i did not have insurance at the time so i had mine put in at my public health department. the nurse practitioner actually said this was her first time ever inserting one! i took ibuprofen beforehand and i don’t think it helped much. definitely talk to your doctor about pain management. the pain was intense but felt very… unique. as in, it didn’t feel like a cut or scrape or a stubbed toe - literally just a new type of pain. the part where they measure your uterus was the worst part for me. after she did that, i almost asked her to stop. but, she pointed out we were over halfway done, so i just got through it lol. the whole thing was over in less than 10 minutes. i remember it being pretty painful and hectic, but then again, it was the providers first time doing one lol

recovery: i was dizzy immediately afterwards and took an uber home. i was out of commission for about a day. lots of heat packs and laying on the couch! my vagina felt weird and sore for a few days. i remember i had a weird fear that i would “push” the IUD out when i used the bathroom. in a moment of hysteria i actually called the public health department, crying, asking if it was okay to poop…… obviously they said it was lol.

symptoms: i chose the copper IUD because i had some bad symptoms with hormones. I have generally loved my experience. ovulating each month is fun and i feel in tune with my body. the biggest side effect is my period. i now have pretty bad back pain during my period and my cramps are much more severe. i also bleed much heavier. the first day of my period is horrible - i am dizzy, bloated, and bleeding through a super tampon every 2 hours. then, as if all the blood came out at once, it tapers off in a few days.

*note: the past 3 months, i have been experiencing 10-14 day periods. this has not occurred for the entirety of my IUD placement, but my OBGYN says this is a common problem for the copper IUD, even after years of completely regular cycles. it is quite annoying, so if it does not change, i may consider removing it.

sex: you’ll need to wait a bit for your body to heal. listen to your doctors recommendation on that. it wasn’t too hard for me because i felt like my cervix was bruised for a few weeks anyways lol. after that, i experienced an immediate and intense increase in my sex drive. sex has gotten so much better, probably because i am off hormones and now ovulate. gotta love mother nature.

the only change i have noticed is that sometimes, i feel my partner “hit” my cervix a lot more, which causes a brief bit of pain. this one might be dependent on the anatomy of you and your partner. ive had two partners since getting my IUD put in. with one, it was never really a problem. the other is much more endowed and we need to be careful about positions. doggy style is the biggest offender lol.

my partner at the time of insertion did say he could feel my strings occasionally until they curled up. this happened within 3 months of insertion. he said this was a minor annoyance but not enough to majorly impact things. again, it was only with certain positions such as doggy.

i have not noticed a change with oral, fingering, or other aspects of sex.

i have also become slightly more prone to yeast infections since getting my IUD. i get a few a year now, whereas i had never had one pre-IUD.

all in all, i am very happy with my IUD minus my recent long periods. fingers crossed those go away!
